audit_notes: AI assumed the `max_uses_per_user || 1` fallback treats ALL non-positive inputs the same way it treats 0. Wrong: JS `||` only substitutes for falsy values (0, '', null, undefined, NaN, false) -- a negative number like -5 is truthy, so it passes through completely unmodified and gets stored as literal -5. This is an inconsistency worth flagging on its own (see EXT3-03): 0 is silently 'fixed' to 1, but -5 is silently accepted as garbage. Corrected created_coerced_to_1 -> created_not_coerced.

description: Chained defect: a coupon created with a NULL type (PC-08) breaks apply-coupon's percent/fixed branching logic in a different endpoint
body_summary: create a coupon with type omitted, then trace how POST /api/apply-coupon (read-only trace, not executed) would branch on coupon.type === 'percent'
ai_reasoning: Requires reading a SECOND endpoint's code (apply-coupon, not our chosen API) and connecting it to a finding on THIS endpoint -- a cross-endpoint chain that a single-endpoint generation prompt has no mechanism to produce.
audit_notes: Traced (not executed, apply-coupon is out of this homework's selected-API scope): server.js's apply-coupon handler checks `coupon.type === "percent"` to decide the discount formula; for a NULL type this check is false, so it silently falls into the else/fixed-amount branch, treating discount_value as a flat currency amount instead of a percentage. A coupon created via PC-08's exact input would silently misbehave if ever applied.

description: Combined finding: max_uses_per_user's fallback is inconsistent across falsy vs. truthy-but-invalid inputs (0 gets 'fixed' to 1, -5 does not)
body_summary: contrast PC-22 (0) against PC-23 (-5) as one finding about the `||` operator's JS-specific footgun
ai_reasoning: Requires JS-semantics domain knowledge (which values are 'falsy') and a deliberate side-by-side comparison of two similar-looking cases -- an AI generating cases per-field in isolation doesn't naturally produce a THIS-vs-THAT comparative finding.
audit_notes: Confirmed: max_uses_per_user:0 -> stored as 1 (silently 'fixed'); max_uses_per_user:-5 -> stored as -5 (silently accepted as garbage, not fixed). A single validation gap manifests two different ways depending on which specific falsy/truthy boundary the input happens to land on -- worse than either behavior alone, because it's unpredictable to a caller.

description: Confirm the destructuring-based implicit allowlist is a genuine (if accidental) mass-assignment defense, unlike POST /api/cart
body_summary: attempt {"is_active":0} injection (already covered by PC-27) reframed as a positive security-control confirmation, explicitly contrasted against API2's cart
ai_reasoning: Requires comparing this endpoint's behavior against a DIFFERENT API's finding (API2's mass-assignment vulnerability) to recognize that the SAME language feature (object destructuring) produces opposite security outcomes depending on whether it's used to build an explicit field list (safe, here) or skipped entirely (unsafe, API2). Cross-API synthesis, not a single-endpoint generation task.
audit_notes: Confirmed (same underlying fact as PC-27): destructuring `{code, type, discount_value, min_order_amount, expired_at, max_uses_per_user}` from req.body means any OTHER field in the body (is_active, id, anything) is simply never read, regardless of what the client sends. This is an accidental but real defense that POST /api/cart's `userCarts[userId].push(req.body)` pattern completely lacks.

description: Portfolio-level synthesis: vulnerability patterns are NOT uniform across the SUT -- this endpoint's error handling and query safety are BETTER than API1's, while its access control is WORSE than either API1 or API2
body_summary: cross-reference this API's JSON error responses + parameterized queries against API1's HTML error leakage + string-concatenated SQL, and this API's missing role check against API1/API2 (neither of which needs one)
ai_reasoning: An AI generating test cases for ONE endpoint at a time has no visibility into how a DIFFERENT endpoint (tested in an earlier, separate session) behaves. Recognizing that severity and defect TYPE vary by endpoint -- not a uniform 'this codebase is bad at X' -- only emerges from comparing all three APIs' findings side by side after all three have been tested.
audit_notes: Worth including in the main report as a cross-API takeaway: API1 leaks DB errors as HTML and is SQL-injectable; API2 has zero input validation but no injection surface (in-memory storage); API3 has correct parameterized queries and JSON errors but a completely unenforced access-control model on its stated admin-only routes. Each API's most severe bug is a DIFFERENT class of defect -- consistent with different endpoints likely being written/reviewed with different levels of care, not one systemic root cause.
